# Anatomy of a batch job {#sec-anatomy}

::: {.tldr}
A batch job is a shell script with `#SBATCH` directives at the top. The one directive you
**cannot** omit is `--account=<project>` — your project name, not your username. Submit with
`sbatch`, and Slurm writes output to `slurm-<jobid>.out`.
:::

## The smallest useful job

Here is a complete, working submit script. Save it as `submit.sh`:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --account=cowy-firesurro     # WHO PAYS — the one you can't omit
#SBATCH --job-name=hello
#SBATCH --time=00:10:00              # 10 minutes; jobs are killed at the limit
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=1
#SBATCH --mem=4G                     # always set memory explicitly (see below)
#SBATCH --output=slurm-%j.out        # %j is replaced by the job ID

echo "Running on host: $(hostname)"
echo "Job $SLURM_JOB_ID started at $(date)"

module purge
module load gcc/14.2.0 python/3.12.0

python my_analysis.py

echo "Finished at $(date)"
```

Submit it:

```bash
sbatch submit.sh
# Submitted batch job 123456
```

Watch it and read the output:

```bash
squeue --me                 # is it pending / running?
tail -f slurm-123456.out    # follow output as it's written
```

That's the whole loop: write script → `sbatch` → watch → read output. Everything else is
refinement.

## The one directive you cannot omit

```bash
#SBATCH --account=cowy-firesurro
```

::: {.callout-important}
## `--account` is your *project*, not your username
Every job on MedicineBow **must** specify an account, and it's the *project* name
(`cowy-firesurro`), not your login name. Leave it out and the job is rejected immediately.
This is the single most common first error. Confirm your exact project name with your PI
(@sec-account) and put it in every script — or set it once as a default:

```bash
# add to ~/.bashrc so you never forget it
export SBATCH_ACCOUNT=cowy-firesurro
```

Even so, keep `--account` in the script itself — it documents intent and survives being run
by a collaborator whose default differs.
:::

## Anatomy, directive by directive

| Directive | What it does | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `--account` | which project pays | **required** |
| `--job-name` | label in the queue | makes `squeue` readable |
| `--time` | wall-clock limit | job is **killed** at this limit — pad it a bit |
| `--partition` | which hardware pool | default is `mb`; see @sec-partitions |
| `--qos` | urgency/limits tier | default is `normal`; see @sec-partitions |
| `--cpus-per-task` | CPU cores | see @sec-resources |
| `--mem` | memory for the job | **always set this** — see below |
| `--output` | where stdout/stderr go | `%j` = job ID, `%x` = job name |
| `--mail-type`, `--mail-user` | email on events | `END,FAIL` is a sane choice |

`#SBATCH` lines must come **before any real commands** — the first non-comment, non-`#SBATCH`
line ends the directive block. After that, it's just a bash script that runs on the compute
node.

## Set memory explicitly — always

::: {.callout-warning}
## The 10 GB-per-core memory trap
On the default `mb` partition, if you don't set `--mem`, Slurm gives you **10 GB per CPU
core** (`DefMemPerCPU=10000`). So this innocent-looking request:

```bash
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8       # and no --mem line
```

silently asks for **80 GB of RAM** — and then you queue behind a number you never typed,
because 80 GB is harder to schedule than the 8 GB you probably needed. **Always set `--mem`
(whole-job) or `--mem-per-cpu` explicitly.** This is covered in depth in @sec-resources.
:::

## Making the environment reproducible

A batch job starts in a clean-ish environment. Build the environment you need *inside the
script* so it runs the same way every time and doesn't depend on what you happened to have
loaded when you hit submit:

```bash
module purge
module restore firestack        # a saved module set (see @sec-modules)
# or, for conda:
module load miniconda3/24.3.0
conda activate fire
```

## Useful variables inside a job

Slurm sets environment variables your script can use:

```bash
$SLURM_JOB_ID          # the job's ID
$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK   # cores you were given — pass to your program's thread count
$SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID   # which array element this is (see @sec-arrays)
$SLURM_SUBMIT_DIR      # the directory you ran sbatch from
```

A common pattern is to match your program's threads to what Slurm gave you:

```bash
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=$SLURM_CPUS_PER_TASK
```

Now that you can submit a job, the next two chapters are about doing it *well*: asking for
the right resources (@sec-resources), and choosing the right queue (@sec-partitions).
